Respiratory energetics in Meriones meridianus have been quantified through standard basal metabolic rate determinations, revealing that the maximum oxygen consumption of resting individuals reaches 61.20 milliliters per hour [JOi = 61.20 milliliters per hour] when measured at a stable body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively elevated metabolic rate, characteristic of small desert-dwelling gerbillines, supports a rapid pace of life that is reflected in the species' reproductive timing. For comparison, the maximum reproductive output of females is achieved when they produce litters containing an average of 5.6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5.6 pups per litter], with the capacity to deliver approximately 3 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters each year] under optimal conditions. These two components together yield an exceptionally high annual fecundity that compensates for the substantial predation pressure typical of arid environments. The coordination between high maternal metabolic expenditure and prolific breeding underscores a life-history strategy oriented toward maximizing recruitment during brief windows of resource abundance.

Neonatal body mass has been documented at 3.35 grams [Wwb = 3.35 grams], a value that places the newborn pups among the smaller offspring relative to adult female size within the genus. This modest birth weight likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the short gestation period of 23 days [tg = 23 days] measured at a maternal core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a developmental interval typical of small murid rodents. The rapid embryogenesis required to complete organogenesis within such a compressed timeframe results in altricial neonates that are entirely dependent on maternal care. Field studies have noted that the immediate postpartum period is critical, as the pups must quickly attach to teats and begin suckling to maintain thermal homeostasis. The combination of low birth mass and abbreviated uterine development suggests a trade-off between maternal investment per offspring and the number of young that can be successfully gestated and reared during a single breeding episode.

The weaning period marks a pivotal transition in the early life of Meriones meridianus, with nutritional independence achieved at 21 days after birth [tx = 21 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively early weaning age reflects the high metabolic demands placed on lactating females, who must balance energy expenditure with the need to prepare for subsequent reproductive cycles. Behavioral observations indicate that weanlings begin consuming solid food items such as seeds and insect matter while still intermittently nursing, facilitating a gradual dietary shift. The post-weaning phase is characterized by accelerated somatic growth, during which juveniles rapidly increase in body mass and develop the physiological capacity for independent thermoregulation. Survival during this period is strongly influenced by environmental productivity, with cohorts born during peak vegetation seasons exhibiting markedly higher recruitment rates than those from litters produced under harsh drought conditions.

Sexual maturation proceeds swiftly following weaning, with individuals attaining puberty at 61 days after birth [tp = 61 days after birth] when maintained at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This remarkably short interval between weaning and reproductive readiness underscores a life-history adaptation to unpredictable desert environments, where the ability to breed during the same season of birth can confer a substantial demographic advantage. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue confirm that spermatogenesis in males and follicular development in females are complete by this age, enabling copulation and fertilization to occur soon after the pubertal transition. The rapid maturation is accompanied by continued increases in body size, as young females have not yet attained the ultimate adult mass of 60 grams [Wwi = 60 grams] that characterizes fully grown reproductively active females. This decoupling of somatic and reproductive maturation allows individuals to begin contributing to population growth while still investing in their own structural development.

Adult female body mass in Meriones meridianus exhibits considerable variation, but the ultimate wet weight for fully grown individuals stabilizes at approximately 60 grams [Wwi = approximately 60 grams], a value consistent with the upper range documented for the species. This asymptotic mass is achieved through a combination of skeletal elongation and fat deposition that continues well beyond the onset of reproductive activity. Longevity records from both wild populations and captive colonies indicate that the maximum lifespan spans approximately 6.8 years [am = approximately 6.8 years] when measured at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a relatively extended duration for a rodent of this body size. The prolonged lifespan relative to expectation based on mass alone may reflect adaptations to reduce the risk of starvation during extended droughts, allowing individuals to persist through multiple seasons of low resource availability. Comparative analyses with related gerbil species suggest that the combination of moderate adult body size, early maturation, and substantial longevity positions Meriones meridianus as a slow-fast life-history continuum strategist well suited to the stochastic productivity pulses of Central Asian deserts.
